members.note: EDreamPanelHorizontalAlignment. On the control rather than in the style: where a thing sits is that thing's business, and two borders sharing a sheet hold different things.

On the PANEL spelling of a border, on by default as UMG's is: while the border's widget is disabled (its own switch or an ancestor's, UDreamWidget::GetIsEnabledInHierarchy) the background -- the owning widget's visual -- draws at 45% of its alpha, which is what SBorder's disabled draw effect comes to in the default Slate shader. Only the background: what the border holds shows its own disabled look.

Colour and alpha both, as the content hole's content tint (UDreamWidget::SetContentTint): every visual below the hole is multiplied by it in linear space on its way to the screen, as SCompoundWidget blends its ColorAndOpacity into what its children paint with, and the border's own face is never tinted. Nothing inside is written to, and the content's RenderOpacity is left free for whatever fades it. UDreamLayoutContainerBorder::ContentColorAndOpacity is the same on the panel spelling.
In the style, because it is one quantity and a second copy on the control is how the two learn to disagree. GetPadding answers the RESOLVED number; SetPadding edits this instance's style.
FDreamUIFaceBrush rather than FSlateBrush -- a control face is a procedural rect, and the brush is its body texture. See the struct's own note.
FColor, and a TINT over the style's background colour -- which is what it is in Slate too.

On the PANEL spelling of a border, where it already scales what the panel reports (MeasureLayout multiplies the result and arranges the content in the rect it actually got -- UBorder's rule exactly). The control lays its face and its content out with an overlay of its own rather than through that panel; a project that needs the report scaled uses the panel, or wraps the control in one.

On the PANEL spelling of a border, off by default as UMG's is: while it is on and the border lays out right to left, the background -- the owning widget's visual -- is mirrored about its own centre by a run-time UDreamMeshModifierMirror, as SBorder draws its brush through a (-1, 1) render transform. The content is not mirrored by it: where the content sits is the panel's to mirror, and every panel that arranges through CommitChildRect already reflects its children across its width under a right-to-left flow (UDreamWidget::FlowDirectionPreference).

A multicast carrying UDreamPointerEventData, not UMG's FEventReply-returning single binding: nothing in this event system asks a handler per call whether the event carries on. That answer is one property for all four -- bConsumeMouseEvents, which is UUIEventTrigger::AllowEventBubbleUp inverted. Gated on bReportMouseEvents, off by default, because a listening border is a consuming border.

Fed by the DRAG seam: this event system reports a moving pointer to the element it pressed on, which is the only motion a border can honestly claim. A hover that never pressed is OnPointerEnter/Exit, which UMG spells elsewhere.

Said at the SECOND PRESS and in place of OnMouseButtonDownEvent for it, as UBorder's is: the event system routes the second press of a double click to the double click and not to the down, which is Slate's FSlateApplication::ProcessMouseButtonDoubleClickEvent. So a double click is one down, one double click and two ups. What counts as a double is the event system's own rule (its DoubleClickTime, the same widget and button, and a second press within the pointer's drag threshold of the first -- the desktop's double-click rectangle and drag threshold are the same few pixels), not a second rule here that could disagree with it.
Colour and alpha both, straight onto the content hole's content tint, as the property above.
Pushed straight onto the content slot.
Takes FDreamUIFaceBrush; see Background above for why that is not FSlateBrush.

USlateBrushAsset wraps an FSlateBrush, which a procedural rect face cannot draw. The two things this framework's face brush takes -- a texture and an atlas sprite -- are what SetBrush and SetBrushFromTexture take.
Replaces the image and leaves the nine-slice, the scale mode and the tint where they were.

A procedural rect has no material of its own to set. Its material is GetMaterialToCreateGeometry -- the shared one the canvas batches every rect with -- and there is no per-instance override anywhere on UDreamVisual (the CustomUIMaterial the comments mention is a leftover name from the upstream library; nothing in this plugin declares it). The two visuals that do carry a material, UDreamText and UDreamImage, are what a material-drawn face is: put one inside the border. SetBrushFromSprite is here instead, which is the thing this face CAN take and Slate cannot.
See bShowEffectWhenDisabled: the background's alpha follows at once.

A rect has no material instance of its own: it draws through its draw call's material, whose parameters the canvas answers through a render-thread proxy shared with every other widget batched into the same call. There is nothing to hand out that setting a parameter on would recolour this border alone.
See DesiredSizeScale above.
UBorder has no style struct at all; this is the family's spelling of replacing a look at runtime.
